bull_bear.body:
- Second largest corn wet miller / maize-based specialty products manufacturer in India, giving scale that is the precondition for moving into modified starches and derivatives
- Plants sited deliberately close to the maize belt and to ports (Hazira, Nhava Sheva, Mundra, Kandla), shortening both the inbound and outbound logistics chain
- Strong farmer sourcing ecosystem: 30% of maize sourced direct from local farmers plus mandi and stockist channels, backed by 50,000 MT storage at Dhule that buffers seasonal swings
- Certification stack (USFDA, HACCP, FSSC 22000, ISO 9001:2015, SGS, Kosher, Halal, APEDA) that underpins qualification with pharmaceutical and overseas food customers
- Export-led model spanning 41 countries with reduced regional concentration — Asia's share of the export book fell from 68% to 49% during FY 2025-26
- In-house R&D at Ahmedabad translating technical depth into differentiated, higher-margin products
- Expansion-ready infrastructure: land and infrastructure available at the expanded manufacturing platform to support future growth
- Diversified application base across 13+ functional applications and four product families from a single maize feedstock, with wet milling turning co-products into revenue rather than waste
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price volatility and single-input dependence on maize — Dependence on maize exposes the Company to fluctuations in crop yields, weather conditions, seasonal availability and procurement prices; any disruption in availability or procurement may affect production schedules, inventory levels and manufacturing costs. This is structural: every product family is derived from one feedstock, so maize is both the cost base and the volume constraint.
- Agricultural and climate risk to the maize crop — Adverse weather conditions and variations in maize production may affect raw-material availability, quality and procurement costs. Management explicitly lists climatic conditions among the factors it remains mindful of in its Outlook.
- Competitive intensity in a commoditised native starch market — The Company operates in a competitive industry with domestic and international manufacturers; increasing competition may exert pressure on pricing, customer retention, product differentiation and market share. The Chairman describes the environment as genuinely competitive and declines to date any recovery in native starch pricing.
- Market and pricing volatility across end-use industries — Fluctuations in demand and pricing across end-use industries may impact sales volumes, product realisations and overall market conditions — visible in FY 2025-26, when revenue from operations fell while the Company describes a particularly challenging first half since listing.
- Export concentration and foreign exchange exposure — Exports contributed 34% of revenue across 41 countries, so export transactions expose the Company to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates and adverse currency movements may affect export realisations and profitability. Regional concentration is being actively reduced — Asia's share of the export book fell from 68% to 49% — but remains a structural exposure.
- Global market and trade conditions — Changes in international trade policies, geopolitical developments, freight costs and global market conditions may affect export competitiveness and demand across certain markets; the Board's risk framework specifically monitors geopolitical developments affecting supply chains, export-import regulations and energy pricing.
- Execution and utilisation risk on the expanded capacity — Total installed capacity more than doubled from 1,100 TPD to 2,350 TPD with the derivatives facility still to be commissioned in FY 2026-27; capacity utilisation was 73% in FY 2025-26, so earnings now depend on converting a much larger fixed asset base into volume, and management flags the need for continuous investment in product development and process capability as customer requirements evolve.
- Availability and adoption of substitute ingredients — The availability and adoption of alternative ingredients for certain applications may affect demand for specific starch-based products, a risk that grows as the Company shifts revenue toward application-specific speciality grades.
- Energy and logistics cost inflation — Management states it remains mindful of energy and logistics costs alongside maize price volatility; wet milling is energy-intensive and the export model is freight-exposed, partially mitigated by 6.6 MW solar and a 1.6 MW biogas plant and by plant proximity to major ports.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Sanstar Limited is an integrated manufacturer of maize-based specialty products and ingredient solutions, wet milling maize into native starch, modified starches, derivatives and sweeteners, and associated co-products. It sells into food and beverages, pharmaceuticals, paper and packaging, textiles, adhesives, personal care, animal nutrition and other industrial applications. Manufacturing sits at Dhule (Maharashtra) and Kutch (Gujarat), with an R&D centre at Ahmedabad, serving customers across India and 41 countries; the company reports a single operating segment under Ind AS 108.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Specialty Starches:** Native Maize Starch, Dextrin, San O Gel, Sanocat, Sano Spray, Sanolose B, Sanosize, Sanalox M
- **Derivatives & Sweeteners:** Maltodextrin, HMCS, Dextrose Monohydrate, Sorbitol, Corn Fiber, Liquid Glucose
- **Co-Products:** Corn Steep Liquor, Corn Germ, Corn Gluten Feed, Corn Gluten Meal (60%) / Maize Gluten Meal

outlook.body:
- Completing the derivatives step: move further up the value chain into derivatives and specialised ingredient applications, where liquid glucose, dextrose and other specialty starch-based ingredients carry more stable pricing than native starch and sit closer to the customer's finished product
- Converting capacity into utilisation: ramp up utilisation of the expanded manufacturing platform, improve operating efficiencies and capture operating leverage from capacity already commissioned
- Widening the export base: expand participation across international markets and reduce dependence on individual regions, after Asia's share of the export book fell from 68% to 49% in FY 2025-26
- Deepening the sourcing advantage: build on farmer relationships, multi-channel procurement through mandis and stockists, and storage infrastructure to secure raw-material availability, quality and procurement flexibility
- Disciplined cost management and cost-optimisation initiatives expected to strengthen financial performance over the medium to long term
- Strengthening the risk framework alongside expansion — enhancing internal controls, supply-chain resilience and customer credit monitoring, embedding ESG risk into strategic decisions, and monitoring geopolitical developments affecting supply chains, export-import regulations and energy pricing
- Using R&D at Ahmedabad to translate technical depth into differentiated, higher-margin products as the company moves toward pharmaceutical-grade and specialty applications
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The defining project of FY 2025-26 was the expansion of native starch manufacturing capacity at the Dhule (Maharashtra) facility, funded from the proceeds of the Company's Initial Public Offering. At the time of the IPO the Company had committed to a 1,000 TPD expansion of native starch capacity at Dhule; it commissioned 1,250 TPD, taking total installed capacity from 1,100 TPD to 2,350 TPD on total project capex of approximately ₹225 crores, of which ₹181.6 crore came from IPO proceeds. The Directors' Report records that the expanded capacity was commissioned on 12th May, 2026 — after the balance-sheet date — and that the associated derivatives facility is expected to be commissioned during FY 2026-27. That derivatives step is management's stated 'next rung': liquid glucose, dextrose and other specialty starch-based ingredients that carry more stable pricing than native starch and sit closer to the customer's finished product. The Company describes itself as having expansion-ready infrastructure, with land and infrastructure available at the significantly expanded manufacturing platform to support future growth, and reports capacity utilisation of 73% and capex during the year of ₹225 crore in its value-creation model. Manufacturing remains two SCADA-automated wet milling facilities at Dhule (2000 TPD) and Kutch, Gujarat (350 TPD), across 110 hectares of land with 50,000 MT of raw-material storage at Dhule, supported by a 2,200 sq ft R&D facility at Ahmedabad, 6.6 MW of solar power capacity and a 1.6 MW biogas plant. Post year-end the Company also raised ₹198.27 crores through a preferential allotment of 1,80,24,157 equity shares to Corn Products Development Inc. at ₹110 per share, with a Nominee Director inducted onto the Board.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management expects better diversification and greater stability in margins as the derivatives facility comes online and value-added products contribute more to the mix
- Native starch pricing is expected to ease as global trade flows normalise, though management explicitly declines to put a date on that recovery and describes the environment as genuinely competitive
- The second half of FY 2025-26 saw plant utilisation improve, production normalise and market conditions stabilise across both facilities, setting a stronger base heading into FY 2026-27
- Domestic demand across food, beverage and pharmaceutical end-uses held firm, with the Indian starch and derivatives market pointing to ~7.3% annual growth over the medium term, led by clean-label formulation trends and expanding pharmaceutical applications
- Industry shift towards speciality, modified and functional starches, driven by customer focus on product consistency, functionality and application-specific performance
- India's corn and corn starch derivatives market is estimated to grow from approximately US$4.63 billion in 2022 to approximately US$8.00 billion by 2030, a CAGR of approximately 7.1% during 2023-2030 (Grand View Research)
- Maize consumption for starch production in India is expected to grow at around 5-6% over the next few years, with roughly 7 million tonnes of maize used for starch production in FY 2025-26
- A strong domestic maize production base and rising demand across food, feed and industrial end-uses provide a favourable foundation for downstream maize processing
- Rising consumption, urbanisation, organised retail and food-service penetration and preference for convenience foods are expected to strengthen demand for value-added food ingredients
- Growing operating leverage as utilisation of the expanded manufacturing base increases; capacity utilisation stood at 73% in FY 2025-26
- Export competitiveness is exposed to international trade policies, geopolitical developments, freight costs and global market conditions
